newsitem.title: USA: Tietmeyer says German growth prospects improved.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says German growth prospects improved.

text.p: The reversal of last year's mark appreciation, a moderate trend in wages, low interest rates and budget consolidation efforts have improved German growth prospects, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said.

"The overall economic situation in Germany, too, has shown a positive trend over the past few months," Tietmeyer said in the text of a speech to be delivered to the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

"Now that last year's excessive appreciation of the D-mark has largely been reversed, and given the present more moderate trend in wages and low interest rates, the Government expects a growth rate above one percent this year, which could increase to 2-1/2 percent in 1997," he said.
"Process in budgetary consolidation and in structural reforms has also improved the medium-term outlook for growth."
But Tietmeyer warned that the improvement was not sufficient to guarantee high, sustained, non-inflationary growth or to reduce high unemployment, which he termed "our most pressing problem."
Tietmeyer noted in his speech that Germany was now taking steps to increase flexibility in the labour market and in wage contracts, in a bid to reduce high labour costs.
"As everywhere, loosening traditional structures is very difficult in Germany, too," he said. "However there is no alternative to this approach."
He said that German monetary policy had played its part in creating the conditions for growth and structural reform, noting that interest rates in Germany were at an all-time low.
